name: Midnight blue
lede: Midnight blue is the blue of the sky at its darkest, a deep violet-leaning navy that Paterson's dictionary says was apparently the correct shade for men's evening dress, before it became a crayon, a screen color and a name for oxidized indigo.

sections.title: A time of day
sections.body: The dictionary gloss is short: an intense blue, apparently the correct shade for men's evening dress [1]. In the books the word shows up in just that setting, as a midnight-blue silk dress laid out beside black lace in a museum case of mourning clothes [2]. Garfield counts 55 color names in one tally that were taken from the time of day, and gives midnight blue as his example [3].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is the CSS and X11 color `MidnightBlue`, hex #191970, one of 140 named colors in the X11 set [1]. Measured, it is very dark and quite saturated: lightness 16, chroma 59 and a hue angle of 303, which is closer to violet than the pure blue its name suggests [4]. ISCC-NBS 1955 calls the region "deep purplish blue" and lists Bellflower, Glory, Monet Blue, Napoleon and Roslyn as names for the neighboring block 197 [4]. The xkcd color survey's own midnight blue, #020035, is far darker still [4]. Its relatives are [[blue]], [[prussian-blue]] and [[indigo]].

sections.title: Out of the indigo vat
sections.body: The best-sourced midnight blue is a dye result. White cloth pulled from an indigo vat changes in the air from yellow through turquoise to midnight blue as the dye oxidizes [5]. Balfour-Paul notes that Islamic courts favored crimson from insect dyes together with midnight blues [6]. In China and elsewhere, indigo-colored paper for Buddhist manuscripts was glazed with rice powder or gypsum, which gave it a lustrous midnight blue [7].

sections.title: A crayon renamed
sections.body: In 1958 the American company Binney & Smith renamed its Prussian blue crayon Midnight Blue, because teachers reported that schoolchildren could not relate to Prussian history [8]. Finlay treats the change as the symbolic end of the Prussian blue era [8].

sections.title: In painting
sections.body: Ball describes the figures of Picasso's *The Absinthe Drinker* and *Old Woman*, both from 1901, as clothed in midnight blues, within the blue world of his early work [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Very dark blues are rare in painting as photographed: only 5 of the 23,531 paintings in the ColorHub archive carry a color this close to midnight blue, 0.02 percent [10].
